prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: temporary accommodation during repairs. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 0)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When the home is still safe to occupy but one room is unusable, I keep temporary accommodation as a last resort and look first at partial-use temporary accommodation as more likely to be necessary, even if the damage itself is limited to one area."},{"type":"preference","content":"When children, older occupants, or anyone with mobility or health needs are involved, I prefer to move quickly on accommodation rather than wait for repairs to be fully scoped, because delay often worsens hardship."},{"type":"observation","content":"When repairs depend on damp-out or drying time after escape of water, I plan for a flexible stay length and avoid promising a fixed return date too early."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the damage is from storm, I check whether the building can be made weather-tight before arranging accommodation, because a secure roof or temporary board-up can remove the need entirely."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the member has pets, I check early whether the accommodation can accept them, because a last-minute refusal can derail the whole arrangement."},{"type":"preference","content":"When a hotel is the quickest safe option, I choose one with simple access to the property and likely repair sites, since long travel adds stress and slows claim progress."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the claim is motor-related and the vehicle is the household’s only practical transport, I treat travel disruption separately from home disruption
